title: How I Long for the Months Gone By
summary: Job remembers his life before disaster: God's friendship over his tent, his children around him, and overflowing abundance. He recalls his honored place at the city gate, where young and old, princes and nobles fell silent before him. He was respected because he rescued the poor, cared for widows and orphans, and broke the power of the unjust. He expected to die in peace, full of days, with his counsel sought like rain.
story: This chapter opens Job's final monologue (chapters 29 to 31), his closing statement before God. Its three parts move like a legal case: chapter 29 describes his past honor, chapter 30 his present humiliation, and chapter 31 his oath of innocence and challenge to God to answer. The friends have fallen silent, and Job now speaks to no one in particular, remembering and lamenting. The chapter also answers Eliphaz's accusations in chapter 22 that Job oppressed widows, orphans, and the poor. Job's memory paints the opposite picture: he was their defender. The reader knows from the prologue (chapter 1) that Job's memory is accurate, and that God himself called him blameless and upright.
historical:
The chapter describes the life of a great man in the ancient Near East, the kind of figure the prologue calls the greatest man among all the people of the East (1:3). Such a man was a landowner, a patron with many dependents, and a leader in the public life of his town. The city gate (verse 7) was the center of that life. In ancient towns the gate complex was a large structure with chambers and benches where elders sat, legal cases were heard, business was transacted, and public announcements were made. Archaeologists have uncovered such gate complexes at a number of Iron Age sites in the land of Israel, and passages such as Ruth 4:1-11 and Deuteronomy 21:19 show them in use for legal business.

The ideal of a leader who defends the vulnerable was widespread. Kings across the ancient Near East claimed to protect widows and orphans, and Israel's law made the same care a religious duty (Exodus 22:22-24; Deuteronomy 24:17-22). Job describes himself as fulfilling this ideal as a private citizen.
cultural:
Honor and shame were central values of ancient society, and this chapter describes a man at the height of honor. When Job came to the gate, young men withdrew out of respect, old men stood up, princes stopped talking, and nobles fell silent (verses 8-10). His words were awaited like rain in a dry land (verse 23), an image that would carry great weight in a region that depended entirely on seasonal rains for its crops. The spring showers, the latter rains of March and April, were crucial for the final ripening of grain.

Job's description of his righteousness uses the image of clothing (verse 14): righteousness clothed him, and justice was his robe and turban. Garments signaled status and office in the ancient world, and the turban was worn by people of rank (the same word is used for a royal diadem in Isaiah 62:3). Job's point is that justice was not something he put on for show but the very identity by which he was known. Images of abundance, steps bathed in cream and rocks pouring out oil (verse 6), are poetic pictures of prosperity, recalling the language of the promised land.
literary: The chapter is a lament in the form of a memory, built with a clear symmetry. It opens and closes with Job's standing in the community. Verses 2-6 recall God's friendship and blessing. Verses 7-10 describe the respect Job received at the gate. Verses 11-17, at the center, explain why: he defended the poor, the orphan, the dying, the widow, the blind, the lame, the needy, and the stranger. Verses 18-20 recall his expectation of a long and peaceful life, using images of a nest, a tree with deep roots, and a bow always renewed. Verses 21-25 return to the gate and his counsel. The chapter begins with longing, How I long for the months gone by, and the Hebrew idiom behind it (literally who will give me) is the same one Job uses elsewhere for his deepest wishes. Its tone of wistful memory sets up the sharp contrast of the next chapter, which begins with But now.

outline.t: The days when God watched over me
A defender of the poor and the helpless
I thought I would die in my nest
My counsel like rain, my presence like a king's

doctrines.note: Job remembers the time when God watched over him, his lamp shone above his head, and the friendship of God rested on his tent (verses 2-4). He sees his past blessing as God's care, not his own achievement, and that makes God's present absence all the more painful.

Job's description of his life reads like a portrait of the righteous person that Israel's law and prophets describe: caring for the poor, widow, orphan, and stranger, and resisting the oppressor. His righteousness is not only personal piety but public justice.

Job's memories include his children around him (verse 5), the children he lost in chapter 1. In the ancient world, as in the Bible generally, children were a sign of God's blessing, and their absence is part of Job's grief.

words.note: Sod, counsel, council, or intimate friendship. It describes a circle of trusted confidants, the kind of close relationship in which secrets are shared. In verse 4 Job remembers when the friendship of God rested on his tent, a remarkably intimate description of his former relationship with God.

Tsedeq, righteousness, rightness, or justice. It is paired with mishpat (justice) in verse 14, a common word pair in the Old Testament for social justice and right order. Job says righteousness clothed him: it was his public identity.

Av, father. Job says he was a father to the needy (verse 16), taking on the role of protector and provider for those who had none. Psalm 68:5 describes God himself as a father to the fatherless, and Job modeled that role in his community.

Malqosh, the spring rain, sometimes called the latter rain. It fell in March and April, just before the harvest, and was essential for the crops. In verse 23 people drink in Job's words like spring showers, eager and grateful.

christ: Job's portrait of the righteous man who is eyes to the blind and feet to the lame, a father to the needy, and a defender of the stranger describes the kind of justice the prophets hoped for in the coming king (Isaiah 11:4; Psalm 72:12-14). When John the Baptist's disciples asked Jesus whether he was the one to come, Jesus pointed to his works: the blind receive sight, the lame walk, and the good news is preached to the poor (Matthew 11:4-5). Jesus did in fullness what Job did in part. The chapter also shows a righteous man who lost everything, and the New Testament describes Christ as one who, though he was rich, became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9). The connection is thematic; Job does not speak of a messiah. But his memory of a just life is a picture of the character that the Gospels see perfected in Jesus.

hard.q: Is Job boasting? He describes his own righteousness and honor at great length.
hard.a: Some readers find the chapter uncomfortable. Job speaks of how others honored him, how princes fell silent before him, and how he sat like a king, and it can sound like pride. Elihu and God will later challenge Job, and some interpreters think this chapter shows why: Job's identity was bound up with his status and his good works. Other readers point out that the chapter is a legal defense, not a boast. Eliphaz accused Job of oppressing the poor (chapter 22), and Job answers by describing what he actually did. The book's narrator and God himself confirm that Job was blameless and upright (1:1, 8). Most interpreters see both elements. Job's account is true and his righteousness was real, yet the chapter also reveals how much his sense of self depended on honor and on being needed. When that was stripped away, he was left with only God, and the book's question is whether that is enough.

questions: Job longs for the days when he felt close to God. Have you experienced a season when God felt near that is now gone? How do you live with that memory?
Job was honored because he defended the poor and helpless. What does your community honor people for, and what does that reveal?
Job's sense of who he was depended heavily on his honor and his work. What would remain of your identity if those things were taken away?
